reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: A solitary benign polyp that arises from the maxillary antrum, passes through its ostium (usually the accessory ostium), and extends back into the choana and nasopharynx
It is most common in children and young adults and is typically unilateral, unlike bilateral ethmoidal inflammatory polyps
Presents with progressive unilateral nasal obstruction that may become bilateral, and a large polyp can be seen or felt in the nasopharynx and occasionally hangs behind the soft palate
It has three parts, an antral part, a part in the nasal cavity, and a choanal part, which explains its dumbbell shape
Nasal endoscopy shows a smooth pale polyp, and computed tomography demonstrates the antral origin and opacified maxillary sinus
The definitive treatment is complete removal including the antral origin, as leaving the maxillary attachment leads to recurrence
Endoscopic sinus surgery with removal of the antral component has largely replaced simple avulsion because it lowers recurrence
A unilateral nasal mass should always be evaluated to exclude more sinister pathology before assuming it is an antrochoanal polyp
reference.pathophysiology: An antrochoanal polyp is thought to originate from a cystic or oedematous swelling of the maxillary antral mucosa, often related to chronic inflammation or an antral cyst. The polyp enlarges within the antrum and then prolapses through the maxillary ostium, most often a widened accessory ostium, into the nasal cavity. Continued growth carries it posteriorly through the choana into the nasopharynx, producing its characteristic dumbbell configuration with a narrow neck at the ostium. It is a benign, single, unilateral lesion and, unlike multiple inflammatory polyps, is only loosely linked to allergy.
additionalDifferentials: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in an adolescent male
Encephalocoele or meningocoele in a midline mass
additionalInvestigations: Nasal endoscopy to characterise the polyp and its posterior extension
Computed tomography of the sinuses to confirm the antral origin and define anatomy for surgery
Biopsy or histology of the excised specimen to confirm the benign nature and exclude neoplasia
Assessment for coexisting sinus disease or allergy where relevant
redFlags: A unilateral nasal mass that bleeds readily, particularly in an adolescent male, suggesting angiofibroma rather than a benign polyp
Rapid growth, bony destruction, orbital or neurological signs suggesting malignancy
A midline mass that could be a meningocoele or encephalocoele before any biopsy
Recurrent unilateral polyp raising suspicion of inverted papilloma or missed antral attachment
reference.prognosis: The lesion is benign and the outlook is very good after complete surgical removal; recurrence is uncommon when the antral origin is fully excised but is more frequent after simple avulsion that leaves the maxillary attachment behind.
pitfalls: Assuming a unilateral mass is a simple polyp and biopsying a vascular angiofibroma or a meningocoele
Removing only the nasal part and leaving the antral origin, leading to recurrence
Overlooking malignancy in an adult with a unilateral nasal mass
Failing to obtain cross-sectional imaging before surgery
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Treat definitively by complete surgical excision, using functional endoscopic sinus surgery to remove the choanal, nasal and antral components together

Ensure the maxillary antral origin is fully removed through a wide middle meatal antrostomy, with canine fossa puncture or a limited Caldwell-Luc approach if the attachment cannot otherwise be reached, since a retained attachment causes recurrence
Obtain preoperative CT of the sinuses to confirm the antral origin and plan the surgical approach
Send the excised specimen for histology to confirm the benign nature and exclude neoplasia
Consider topical intranasal corticosteroids for associated mucosal inflammation, recognising these are adjunctive and not curative
Treat any coexisting sinus disease or allergy, and follow up with nasal endoscopy to detect recurrence
